The virus, known for its viral nucleoprotein, possesses a highly conserved genome consisting of five genes: nucleoprotein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), glycoprotein (G), and the viral RNA polymerase (L). To enter cells, trimeric spikes on the exterior of the virus interact with a specific cell receptor, most likely the acetylcholine receptor. This interaction triggers pinocytosis, allowing the virus to enter the cell via an endosome.

In the acidic environment of the endosome, the virus binds to the membrane, releasing its five proteins and single-strand RNA into the cytoplasm. Once within a muscle or nerve cell, the virus undergoes replication. The L protein transcribes five mRNA strands and a positive strand of RNA from the original negative strand RNA using free nucleotides in the cytoplasm. These five mRNA strands are then used to form proteins.

Moving on to a different topic, I'd like to mention "De duplici copia verborum ac rerum commentarii duo," a rhetoric textbook written by Erasmus during the Renaissance. It was the most often printed rhetoric textbook of the time, with 168 editions between 1512 and 1580. The first part of the book, Verborum, focuses on words and includes 147 variations on "Your letter pleased me very much" and 203 variations on "Always, as long as I live, I shall remember you." The second part, Rerum, focuses on arguments to teach critical thinking and advocacy. Erasmus advised students to practice the rhetorical techniques of copiousness by writing letters to each other arguing both sides of an issue. Other notable works by Erasmus include Opuscula plutarchi (1514), and Apophthegmata Patrum (1500).
